Listen to this article Share Nigeria lost an average of 116,563 barrels a day of potential crude and condensate output in 2025 to outages, leaks and shut-ins, the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) has said. The country’s upstream regulator said damaged export pipelines were the most common cause, according to its annual report. The figure, from NUPRC’s 2025 report, equals roughly 7 percent of the 1.67 million barrels a day the agency says the country produced last year. Annualised, the deferrals come to about 42.5 million barrels that stayed in the ground. The regulator said the main culprits were the Trans Niger Pipeline, the Nembe Creek Trunk Line and the Trans Forcados Pipeline, the arteries that carry onshore and swamp crude to export terminals. Planned maintenance and tanker-loading delays at terminals, which forced operators to shut in wells, also contributed heavily, the report said. Read also: Boost for domestic supply as $700m OB3 pipeline sells first commercial gas Uneven Losses Deferrals swung widely through the year. They were lowest in July, at 25,780 barrels a day, and highest in October, at 172,761. November and December were nearly as bad, at 169,340 and 169,786 barrels a day. March also topped 169,000. The early-year losses came from a mix of incidents. In January, a tank-top, or full storage, at the Pennington terminal forced shut-ins. A fire on a floating production vessel closed the Ajapa field, and an outage on the Olero 18-inch line hit the Olero, Dibi and Opuekeba fields. In February, a fire at the Cawthorne Channel-1 terminal added to the losses. Leaks recurred through the spring and summer. Operators reported delivery-line leaks affecting the Diebu Creek, Nun River and Adibawa fields, and a detected leak on the Tebidaba line curtailed output from the Ogbaibiri and Tuomo fields. The Trans Forcados line leaked again in April and September, and the Trans Niger Pipeline was out in August, hitting Heirs Energies, Renaissance and TotalEnergies’ Nigerian unit. The final quarter was dominated by turnaround maintenance. Operators shut in the Agbami, Erha and Usan deepwater fields in turn, and a fire at the Yoho platform continued to hold back production from the Yoho and Awawa fields. In September, an industrial action by the oil workers’ union PENGASSAN also cut output, the report said. Read also:P Dangote stake makes Kenya Pipeline fourth most valuable firm on NSE The commission put 2025 production at 622.1 million barrels of crude oil and condensate, which it described as a 7.5 percent rise in average output from 2024. It credited new production from awardees of petroleum prospecting licenses, including Naphta Global’s Abiala field, Multisub’s Olure field and Ingentia’s Egbolom field, as well as a monitoring team set up to push toward 1 million barrels a day of added output. Output still ran well below the regulator’s own ceiling. The technical allowable rate for oil alone was about 1.87 million barrels a day for most of the second half of 2025, while monthly average oil production ran between roughly 1.37 million and 1.50 million barrels a day. The commission cautioned that its production figures are unreconciled and shouldn’t be reported as export volumes. The report links part of the problem to security. Of 357 oil spills reported in 2025, 177 were attributed to sabotage, or 49.5 percent, and another 116 had no determined cause. Corrosion accounted for 16 spills and equipment failure for 20. Reconciled data showed 3.33 million barrels of oil theft for the year, with the fourth quarter the worst at 2.19 million barrels. The commission also noted that vandalism of liquids pipelines forced curtailment of associated gas production. Gas delivery to the domestic market suffered too. Operators supplied an average of 2,230 million standard cubic feet a day against an allocation of 2,892 million, or 77 percent, with December the weakest month at 69 percent. Read also: Kenya Pipeline shares jump 53% after Dangote’s stake purchase The deferral data bears on a long-running government goal of lifting output toward 2 million barrels a day. Lost barrels from infrastructure failures cannot be recovered by new licensing rounds or field development alone. The commission said it approved 48 field development plans in 2025, expected to add about 743,830 barrels a day of oil production, with first oil projected between 2026 and 2030. Those new volumes still need a reliable route to market. The report doesn’t quantify the revenue lost to deferrals. It does show the commission collected ₦10.42 trillion in 2025, about 63 percent of its N16.54 trillion target and 20.5 percent below the prior year’s collection. The regulator did not say in the report what it plans to do specifically about pipeline reliability. It did list a stronger enforcement push on other fronts, including warnings that operators who fail to file gas flare elimination plans could face penalties.
